Header: 2026-03-04 15:30 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Jared Kim, Priya Patel, Liam O'Neill (Redwood) — Maya Thompson, Carlos Ruiz, Lena Park, Samir Patel (Nautilus)

Summary (auto): Discussed cost/unit economics for Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Customer has latency SLOs and tight budget; tradeoffs on batching and caching covered. Agreed to exchange artifacts and run benchmark.

[00:00] Jared: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm jared from redwood, and this is priya our solutions eng and liam from csm, uh quick round robin?
[00:06] Maya: hey, maya here, head of ml at nautilus, we've got carlos infra and lena on budgets, samir does model ops
[00:12] Jared: awesome, goal for today is to understand your workload and cost constraints — per token economics, batching levers, and whether hosted/dedicated/private makes sense
[00:24] Priya: quick question — are you running both short prompts and long-context flows? that changes batching and caching behavior a lot
[00:31] Maya: mostly short prompts, 30–120 tokens average, some longer session style prompts occasionally up to 2k tokens for explainer flows, but 85% short
[00:40] Samir: we do streaming for trading signals, need p95 under 120ms for the short path, 50–100 qps sustained during market hours, spike to 300 qps during open
[00:52] Carlos: infra today is mixed — in-house GPU fleet for model evals, inference mostly on a cloud provider endpoints — costs ballooned last quarter, which is why we're re-evaluating
[01:04] Jared: got it, and budget side? lena, can you share constraints?
[01:08] Lena: roughly $40k/month cap for inference ops initially, that includes model costs and infra, we can stretch if roas justifies it but need predictable unit economics
[01:18] Priya: ok that's helpful — on per-token pricing, hosted api is simplest: you're billed per generated and input token, we have stepladders and volume tiers; dedicated reduces unit cost through reserved capacity and autoscaling policies; private is more about control and data residency but has higher fixed costs
[01:36] Maya: can you ballpark numbers? like top-line per-token on hosted vs dedicated? even a rough ratio helps
[01:42] Jared: rough publicly: hosted per-token can be ~1x baseline for our curated models; dedicated can cut unit cost by 30–60% depending on utilization because of amortized GPU reservations, and private has similar or slightly lower unit cost at high utilization but you pick up infra ops and licensing. i'll follow up with a spreadsheet but roughs are: hosted say $0.0009 per token for typical model, dedicated $0.0004–0.0006 at 70–90% utilization
[02:06] Lena: that helps, main question is how to get our effective cost below $0.0007/token given our 40k budget and expected token volume
[02:15] Priya: batching and caching are the big levers. for short prompts batching improves throughput and reduces per-token kernel overhead; prefix/KV cache can remove repeated context cost for session-based flows, especially if you have lots of repeated system prompts or few-shot examples
[02:28] Samir: we do a lot of repeated system prompts — trading rules, so prefix caching could be a big win. is that auto in redwood or does it need code changes?
[02:36] Priya: we have automatic prefix & KV caching at the runtime level for compatible models; you can also control cache TTLs and consult keys. some work to tag requests but often minimal SDK changes — we can show code examples in the benchmark
[02:46] Maya: what about batching latencies — if we batch to improve cost, do we blow past 120ms p95?
[02:52] Priya: it's workload dependent. continuous batching tries to flush quickly for low-latency flows; you can set max batch delay, size thresholds. in practice for 30–120 token flows you can get batching gains without breaching p95 if you tune target latency. we can run experiments in the perf bench to measure tradeoff with your req distribution
[03:12] Carlos: curious about quantization — do you support int8 or 4-bit? what impact on latency/cost/quality?
[03:19] Priya: yes we onboard quantized variants — int8 and Q4 depending on model family. quantization reduces memory and increases GPU throughput so it can lower unit compute cost; quality impact is model-dependent. for customer-critical flows we recommend A/B tests and quality regression evals. we can include quantized variants in the benchmark run
[03:33] Maya: ok, when you say dedicated lowers unit cost by 30–60% that's assuming high utilization — how sensitive is that to our diurnal spikes and market-open burst?
[03:42] Jared: good call — dedicated is best when you have predictable sustained throughput; we have autoscaling and burst options to handle spikes but bursts on dedicated can be expensive if you provision too much headroom. there's also routing to hosted as a fallback for overflow, which gives a hybrid approach: reserved capacity + overflow to hosted, balancing SLOs and cost
[04:01] Samir: overflow to hosted — is routing automatic? what about per-request data residency?
[04:07] Priya: routing is policy-driven — you can set fallback models or regions. for strict data residency you'd keep traffic in private/dedicated only; overflow to hosted would cross boundaries so you'd need to be comfortable with that path or use private VPC with peered regions for dedicated
[04:25] Lena: security — SOC2 and KMS for encryption at rest? and audit logs for billing reconciliation?
[04:31] Jared: SOC2 Type II in place, KMS integrations for private deployments, audit logs in the console with token-level cost breakdowns; we'll send the security pack after the call
[04:40] Maya: great. on metrics — we'd like to optimize for cost per inference (per-request rather than per-token sometimes), does redwood provide per-route token breakdowns?
[04:48] Priya: yes console shows per-route model and token cost, P95 latency, token counts, and you can export for your finance team. you can also tag traffic for segmentation
[04:58] Carlos: for benchmark, we can give you a 7-day sample and a set of golden prompts — we'll want Redwood to run both hosted and dedicated runs so we can compare numbers apples-to-apples
[05:08] Jared: absolutely, bench plan: you provide qps histogram, prompt examples, priority routes; we run hosted and dedicated configs (with and without KV cache, and quantized variants) and return latency and cost per token reports; aim to have initial results in one week post-artifact exchange
[05:20] Maya: what's the onboarding time for dedicated if we go that route? days, weeks?
[05:24] Jared: provisioning dedicated pools typically 1–2 weeks depending on region and commit tier; pilot faster if we use smaller reserved capacity for POC. private on-prem longer due to infra and security reviews
[05:34] Lena: what about contracts — monthly commit, annual? flexibility to ramp down?
[05:39] Jared: Dedicated has monthly and annual commit tiers; monthly offers more flexibility but slightly higher unit price; annual is best for bigger discounts. We can model both in the spreadsheet with break-evens given your utilization
[05:51] Samir: any hidden costs? data egress, feature flags?
[05:55] Priya: main costs are token compute and reserved infra. data egress for private setups depends on your cloud; feature flags and console are included, longer retention of logs is an add-on
[06:05] Carlos: curious about model variants — can we pin cheaper quantized variants for lower-cost paths and higher-quality hosted variants for critical requests?
[06:12] Priya: yes, routing and model pinning support that — route by latency, cost, or business rule. you can do A/B rollouts and automatic fallbacks
[06:22] Maya: ok concretely: we project 200M tokens/mo initially. at $0.0009/token that's $180k/mo — way above our $40k cap. what levers get us to ~$0.0002 token or $40k budget?
[06:35] Jared: to hit $0.0002 you'd need very heavy dedup/kv caching and extremely high utilization on dedicated or aggressive quantization and batch tuning; realistically, combining dedicated at 80% util + prefix caching for repeated system contexts + mixed routing could get you to ~$0.0004–0.0005. also consider model architecture changes (smaller tuned models) to drop cost per token
[06:55] Samir: smaller models — we can likely distill several flows into a 7B tuned variant for non-critical paths; critical signals can still hit higher capacity models
[07:03] Lena: ok so a multi-tier approach might be needed: critical low-latency on hosted/high-cost or dedicated high-perf; bulk volume on quantized/dedicated cheaper models
[07:12] Priya: exactly — that's a common pattern, Redwood supports routing policies to implement that. We'll include example config and cost projections in the spreadsheet
[07:22] Carlos: about SLA — if we rely on dedicated for critical flows, what's uptime and latency guarantees?
[07:27] Jared: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency SLOs for enterprise tiers. We can include SLA language in the enterprise package; for pilots it's limited. We'll surface specifics in the follow-up
[07:41] Maya: slightly off-topic but how invasive is SDK change? our platform is python/flask microservices calling current cloud endpoints
[07:47] Priya: minimal — SDK mirrors existing call patterns. For caching you may add headers/tags. We provide examples in python, node, and java. No architecture overhaul for most customers
[07:58] Samir: any gotchas for concurrency and GPU memory? in our tests we saw KV cache sometimes increased memory pressure
[08:05] Priya: true — KV cache increases memory footprint for large context caches; runtime manages eviction and TTLs. We'll test with your prompt sizes and working set in the bench to tune cache sizes vs throughput
[08:18] Lena: can you reiterate deliverables and timeline?
[08:22] Jared: sure — Priya sends bench template and cost-model by 2026-03-06; Maya provides prompt set + qps histogram by 2026-03-09; we'll run hosted and dedicated bench with quantized variants and return results within a week of receiving artifacts; also send security pack immediately after call
[08:38] Maya: sounds good. quick pricing ask — can you put 3 tier sample pricing in spreadsheet: POC (small reserved), Prod-monthly commit, Prod-annual commit with blended per-token numbers?
[08:48] Jared: yes will do. we'll include break-even utilization lines and an example hybrid overflow configuration
[08:54] Carlos: one last thing — are there reference customers in finance/trading space? use cases similar to ours?
[08:59] Liam: yes, we have a few customers in capital markets and low-latency analytic spaces, we'll anonymize references and include a short case study in follow-up
[09:07] Maya: awesome, thanks everyone
[09:10] Jared: thanks all, we'll follow up w the spreadsheet and the security docs, and schedule the perf run after we get artifacts
[09:15] (call ends)
